\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{नापितः} (nāpitaḥ)}{नापितः (nāpitaḥ)}]{\sk{नापितः} (nāpitaḥ) — a barber}

\label{lesson:SA-C148-napitah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a minister, then the Sanskrit for a general.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{नापितः}}
\textbf{\sk{नापितः}} — \emph{nāpitaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a barber\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{nāpita} \textquotedblleft{}a barber\textquotedblright{} is old, in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. CDIAL 13792, after EWA, links it with the root √snā \textquotedblleft{}bathe\textquotedblright{}, through a form \emph{snāpitṛ} \textquotedblleft{}one who bathes others\textquotedblright{}, which MW also queries. It lives on as Hindi \emph{nāū} and \emph{nāī} \textquotedblleft{}barber\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 13792).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nāpitaḥ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{nāpitaḥ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for a minister, then the Sanskrit for a general, then say \emph{nāpitaḥ} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{पाचकः} (pācakaḥ)}{पाचकः (pācakaḥ)}]{\sk{पाचकः} (pācakaḥ) — a cook}

\label{lesson:SA-C148-pacakah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a general, then the Sanskrit for a barber.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{पाचकः}}
\textbf{\sk{पाचकः}} — \emph{pācakaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a cook\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{pācaka} is built from the root √pac \textquotedblleft{}cook, bake\textquotedblright{} with the agent suffix \emph{-aka} (MW): \textquotedblleft{}one who cooks\textquotedblright{}. MW sets √pac beside Latin \emph{coquo} \textquotedblleft{}I cook\textquotedblright{}, the source of English \emph{cook} and \emph{kitchen}, and Greek \emph{pessō}.
\end{cousinweb}

\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{मालाकारः} (mālākāraḥ)}{मालाकारः (mālākāraḥ)}]{\sk{मालाकारः} (mālākāraḥ) — a gardener, a garland-maker}

\label{lesson:SA-C148-malakarah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a barber, then the Sanskrit for a cook.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{मालाकारः}}
\textbf{\sk{मालाकारः}} — \emph{mālākāraḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a gardener, a garland-maker\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{mālākāra} is built from \emph{mālā} \textquotedblleft{}garland\textquotedblright{} and \emph{kāra} \textquotedblleft{}maker\textquotedblright{}, from the root √kṛ \textquotedblleft{}do, make\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 10093): \textquotedblleft{}a garland-maker\textquotedblright{}, and so \textquotedblleft{}a gardener, a florist\textquotedblright{} (MW). CDIAL 10092 takes \emph{mālā} itself from Dravidian.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{धीवरः} (dhīvaraḥ)}{धीवरः (dhīvaraḥ)}]{\sk{धीवरः} (dhīvaraḥ) — a fisherman}

\label{lesson:SA-C148-dhivarah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a cook, then the Sanskrit for a gardener.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{धीवरः}}
\textbf{\sk{धीवरः}} — \emph{dhīvaraḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a fisherman\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dhīvara} \textquotedblleft{}a fisherman\textquotedblright{} appears from the Mahābhārata on, also as the name of a caste (CDIAL 6819). Neither MW nor CDIAL gives a derivation, so its origin is uncertain. It lives on as Hindi \emph{dhīmar} and Punjabi \emph{jhīwar} \textquotedblleft{}fisherman\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 6819).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{गोपालः} (gopālaḥ)}{गोपालः (gopālaḥ)}]{\sk{गोपालः} (gopālaḥ) — a cowherd}

\label{lesson:SA-C148-gopalah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a gardener, then the Sanskrit for a fisherman.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{गोपालः}}
\textbf{\sk{गोपालः}} — \emph{gopālaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a cowherd\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{gopāla} is built from \emph{go} \textquotedblleft{}cow\textquotedblright{} and \emph{pāla} \textquotedblleft{}guard, keeper\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 4293): \textquotedblleft{}the cow-keeper\textquotedblright{}, already in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā. MW sets \emph{go} beside Greek \emph{bous}, Latin \emph{bos} and English \emph{cow}: one inherited Indo-European word.
\end{cousinweb}
